items.name: MMLU
items.measures: Breadth of knowledge and reasoning across 57 academic and professional subjects, from elementary mathematics to law and medicine, using multiple-choice questions.

items.name: GPQA Diamond
items.measures: Graduate-level scientific reasoning in biology, chemistry, and physics, on questions written and validated by PhD-level experts to be hard to answer even with a search engine.

items.name: HumanEval
items.measures: Small-scale Python code generation: writing a correct function body from a docstring.

items.name: LMArena (Chatbot Arena)
items.measures: Human preference: which model people prefer in blind head-to-head conversations, aggregated into Elo-style ratings across categories including coding, math, and creative writing.

items.name: LiveBench
items.measures: Contamination-resistant general capability: math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis, scored against objective ground truth.
items.maintainer: Abacus.AI, NYU, and collaborators (White et al.)

items.name: Humanity's Last Exam
items.measures: Frontier academic reasoning: expert-written questions across more than a hundred subjects, built specifically because MMLU-class tests stopped separating top models.
items.maintainer: Center for AI Safety and Scale AI

items.name: MLPerf Training
items.measures: Time-to-train: how fast a hardware and software system trains reference models, including large language model workloads, to a fixed quality target.

items.name: MLPerf Inference
items.measures: Serving throughput and latency for datacenter and edge systems on standardized workloads, including LLM scenarios with strict latency constraints.

items.name: LLMPerf
items.measures: Real-world serving behavior of LLM endpoints and inference stacks: time to first token, inter-token latency, and throughput under concurrent load.

items.name: MLPerf Client
items.measures: On-device LLM inference performance on consumer hardware: laptops and desktops running local models through vendor acceleration stacks.

items.name: ANN-Benchmarks
items.measures: Approximate nearest neighbor algorithm quality: the recall-versus-queries-per-second trade-off curve for vector search algorithms on standard datasets.

items.name: VectorDBBench
items.measures: End-to-end vector database performance: ingestion, index build, query throughput, latency, and recall across managed services and open-source systems, including filtered search.

items.name: Big ANN Benchmarks
items.measures: Vector search at billion scale, including the hard variants production systems face: filtered queries, streaming updates, out-of-distribution queries, and sparse vectors.

items.name: SWE-bench and SWE-bench Verified
items.measures: Real software engineering: whether an agent can resolve actual GitHub issues from popular Python repositories with a patch that passes the project's held-out tests.
items.maintainer: Princeton NLP (Jimenez et al.); Verified subset with OpenAI

items.name: WebArena
items.measures: Long-horizon web agency: completing realistic multi-step tasks (shopping, forum posting, code hosting, mapping) on self-hosted replicas of real websites.

items.name: GAIA
items.measures: General assistant competence: questions that are conceptually simple for humans but require browsing, tool use, file handling, and multi-step verification to answer correctly.
items.maintainer: Mialon et al. (Meta AI, Hugging Face, AutoGPT)

items.name: OSWorld
items.measures: Real computer use: controlling an actual desktop operating system across applications (browsers, office suites, file managers, code editors) to finish open-ended tasks.
items.maintainer: University of Hong Kong and Salesforce Research (XLANG Lab)

items.name: τ-bench
items.measures: Customer-facing agent reliability: completing retail and airline service tasks in conversation with a simulated user while obeying written policy rules.

items.name: METR Time Horizon
items.measures: The benchmark measures the length of software and reasoning tasks, measured by how long they take human professionals, that a generalist frontier AI agent can complete autonomously with 50% reliability. It records human expert time on diverse multi-step tasks and uses that time to predict model success probability. The resulting time horizon characterizes how long a task a model can handle at a given success rate.

items.name: RE-Bench
items.measures: RE-Bench measures the performance of humans and frontier model agents on ML research engineering tasks. It uses seven environments, each centered on a task such as fitting a scaling law or optimizing a GPU kernel, where agents are given a computer, often with GPUs, a scoring function, and a fixed time limit to score as high as possible. The tasks are designed to require ML research skills such as conducting experiments, implementing solutions, and allocating compute sensibly.

items.name: HCAST
items.measures: HCAST measures the success rates of AI agents on 189 tasks in machine learning engineering, cybersecurity, software engineering, and general reasoning. It calibrates these tasks by how long they take skilled humans, from one minute to 8 or more hours. This provides a grounded metric connecting AI performance to real world effects.

how_to_read: Contamination is the quiet tax on every static benchmark: published questions leak into training corpora, and after a year or two nobody can say how much of a score is capability versus rehearsal. This is why the field keeps building contamination-resistant designs, LiveBench refreshes its questions monthly, SWE-bench Verified was human-screened, Humanity's Last Exam was written fresh by experts, and why a model that shines on old benchmarks but lags on fresh ones deserves suspicion.

Saturation is the benchmark life cycle: a good test separates models for a few years, then the frontier compresses against its ceiling and differences become noise. MMLU and HumanEval have completed the cycle; GPQA is well along it. A saturated benchmark is not useless, it still screens smaller models, but frontier comparisons on it are theater, and each generation of harder benchmarks buys less time than the last.

Goodhart's law runs the leaderboards: when a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring. Vendors optimize for the benchmarks buyers watch, sometimes legitimately, sometimes by testing many private variants and publishing the best, as the Leaderboard Illusion research documented on LMArena. The defense is triangulation, a model that leads on preference votes, static knowledge tests, and contamination-resistant tasks simultaneously is probably good; a model that leads on exactly one is probably optimized.

Agent benchmarks measure pipelines, not models: every SWE-bench, WebArena, or OSWorld score entangles the model with its scaffold, retry budget, and tool access, and leaderboard gaps often reflect harness engineering. Before comparing two numbers, confirm the scaffolds match. And no benchmark number transfers automatically to your workload, the reliable final step is always a pilot on your own tasks, which is precisely what the benchmarks themselves did to the tasks they froze.

items.claim: On Vals AI's independent AIME 2025 evaluation, leading proprietary and open models scored above 85 percent without tools.

maintenance_note: Every benchmark page here carries a last-verified date and sits on a 90-day review cycle: maintainer changes, methodology updates, new criticisms, and saturation status are re-checked against the primary sources and folded in. Corrections land in the database and republish automatically on the next daily site build.
